newsitem.title: UK: IRA wound policeman in daring N.Irish attack.
newsitem.headline: IRA wound policeman in daring N.Irish attack.

text.p: IRA guerrillas wounded a police officer in an audacious daylight missile attack on Northern Ireland's Courts of Justice on Monday, their most spectacular raid in a burgeoning new wave of violence against British rule.

The Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) said one of their officers, who was in a security hut hit by a "PRIG" missile, was treated for damaged ears but was not kept in hospital. He and a woman passer-by also received treatment for shock.

"It was an improvised grenade fired from a launcher," a police source told Reuters after the Irish Republican Army (IRA) struck for the first time in central Belfast since ending a 17-month truce last February.

The "propelled recoilless improvised grenade (PRIG)" -- part of the IRA's armoury of home-made weapons -- was fired from a car passing the heavily protected court complex, the heart of Britain's legal system in the region and regarded by the guerrillas as a prestige target.

A caller using an IRA identity codeword later telephoned a radio station, saying the attack was the work of its so-called "Belfast Brigade" and warning that bombs had also been left at six other points, in hotels and transport termini.
Some two hours afterwards police sources said: "The premises have all been checked and nothing was found."
Security officials believed the alerts were designed to stretch police and army resources to impede efforts to track down the culprits behind the attack at the courts.
The car used in the noon raid had been hijacked by two armed men in a Catholic part of central Belfast. The guerrillas set fire to it later to destroy forensic evidence.
The "PRIG" was fired from inside the stolen car. The injured policeman dived for cover as he saw a rear window of the vehicle being slowly wound down, according to security sources.

Protestant politician Ken Maginnis, security spokesman for the province's chief pro-British party, the Ulster Unionists, said the attack had put paid to any notion that recent IRA operations had been purposely botched as part of a "phoney war" aimed at demonstrating its potential for action.

Britain says the IRA must abandon its 27-year campaign of violence to oust Britain from Northern Ireland to win a seat for its Sinn Fein political arm in current multi-party talks on the future of the province.
"After so many false dawns it is now generally accepted by realists within both the (British) government and opposition that Sinn Fein/IRA is irredeemable," Maginnis told Reuters.
Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said he was committed, with others, to create conditions for an end to violence on all sides, which he termed "regrettable symptoms" of a political deadlock.
The attack was widely seen as a further blow to lingering hopes that the IRA might call a ceasefire in the run-up to a general election that Britain must hold by May at the latest.

On New Year's Eve, IRA guerrillas dumped a 1000 lb (450 kg) car bomb in the grounds of historic Belfast Castle. Police said it was intended to cause "mass murder" among security forces called to deal with the device, which was later disarmed.
Earlier IRA gunmen wounded a Protestant politician's police bodyguard and there have been recent cases of bombs being found and attacks foiled by security forces.

Protestant extremists, who have fought to keep Northern Ireland British, are suspected of two retaliatory attacks on senior Republicans and the missile raid added to fears of a backlash by "Loyalist" militants.
But Gary McMichael, a leader of the political arm of the Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF), a banned Loyalist guerrilla group, insisted that its two-year-old truce was still in operation.
"Speculation about the conditions which would end the Loyalist ceasefire are premature and unhelpful," he said.
